lines.text: Slow week. You'd think a man who buys rime shards would be up to his collar in them, the way the walls have been.
You've run out?
Somebody's taking what the frost leaves. They aren't selling.
I'd try the old burying ground. The ground's been turned over up there, and nobody's died.
I'll have a look.
A fresh mound, no bigger than a loaf. A rime shard sits in the top of it, pressed in neatly, still cold.
Somebody's been careful with this.
Another mound, packed down hard. Another shard. Something wide has been dragged through the grass between the two.
A third, at the back of the ground. The drag marks go on past it, and in under a fall of old stone.
Heavy, whatever it is. And it knows where it's going.
A fall of old stone fills the cleft from side to side. Cold air comes through the gaps.
Earth remembers how it was stacked. Let's see if it'll unstack.
Rime shards, hundreds of them, laid in rows with every point the same way. Under the last row, wrapped in oilcloth, a pair of old gloves, stiff with dirt.
Someone left these here on purpose. I'll take good care of them.
A beetle the size of a calf. It's been burying your shards, in rows.
Has it now.
There are hundreds left. Shall I bring them down?
No. Leave them be.
Let it work. It's cheaper than I am.
You won't say why.
Fair prices, Eldwin. I said fair. I never said open.
A great flat slab, bigger than a door. No name at the head of it. Rows and rows of small strokes, then a ruled line, and nothing written under the line.
A sum, left open.
Cold comes up around the edges. The slab begins to lift.
The slab lies flat again. Under the ruled line, one stroke is fresh.
There's a slab in the old burying ground with a sum cut in it.
Is it paid?
It lay back down.
Then somebody paid. Ask me who some other year.
